# Premortem Playbook

Most agent runs that go badly fail in a small number of recognizable
ways. The point of this document isn't to walk you through a
procedure — it's to name those failure modes and tell you, for each,
the cheapest thing you can do to avoid it. Read this as a checklist
of regrets you don't want to have at the end of the run.

The work itself is straightforward: figure out what the task is,
gather the data the task needs, do the work, and leave a trace
useful to whoever runs next. The reason runs fail isn't that this
sequence is hard — it's that one of the failure modes below catches
people every time.

---

## Setup

Before any of the failure modes apply, you need to know what's
actually around you. Three calls cover most of it. Run them in
parallel:

- `GET http://localhost:8090/health` — what's up.
- `GET http://localhost:8090/openapi.json` — the endpoint map. All
  subsequent calls flow from this. If a path or field isn't in
  here, you don't know it.
- `cat /workspace/learned/*.md` if it's populated — recipes from
  earlier runs. Use them as-is when they cover what you need.

If any of these come back empty, missing, or different from what
you expected, treat that as a real signal — don't paper over it
and proceed on assumption.

---

## Failure 1 — You wrote down something that wasn't there

This is the single most common kill. An ID that wasn't in the
data, a name attached to the wrong person, a quote that's almost
right but not quite, a status that looks plausible but you didn't
read it. Once it's in the output, no later check catches it.

The practice: every concrete value you emit — name, ID, subject,
timestamp, number, status, exact quote — should be a literal copy
of something you actually read, not a reconstruction. Paraphrase
prose freely; never paraphrase a fact. If a piece you'd usually
include isn't in the data, say it isn't, or leave it out. Half an
honest answer beats a complete invented one.

---

## Failure 2 — You acted before you looked

You jumped on the first item the task mentioned, started writing,
and only later noticed the conflict in the calendar, the duplicate
already in the tracker, or the thread that had already resolved
the question. Now your output is wrong in a way that's expensive
to retract.

The practice: before you act, sweep the data you've already pulled
for things that touch each other. Two sources disagreeing.
Something already tracked that you'd be duplicating. Two events on
the same slot. An open item past its window. Surface or resolve
those first; build on top of them second.

---

## Failure 3 — You told the wrong person the wrong thing

Internal specifics ended up in an external message. A codename or
ticket number landed in a channel that broadcasts widely. A
leadership update got operational implementation detail it didn't
ask for. Confidential context leaked into a draft for someone
outside the room.

The practice: classify who reads what before you write. People
doing the same hands-on work as you can hold the operational
detail. People whose role is oversight want trajectory, risk, and
the next checkpoint — not implementation. People outside the
group, and channels where you can't list who's reading, get only
what they already see plus what's about to change. When in doubt
about a proper noun in an outward-facing draft, replace it with a
neutral phrase. When in doubt about a recipient, drop them.

---

## Failure 4 — You promised something you can't be held to

"We'll get back to you soon." "An update is coming shortly." "I'll
take care of this ASAP." These look like commitments. They aren't.
They make the next reader unable to tell whether anything actually
happens.

The practice: every promise carries a specific time, a bounded
window, or a scheduled checkpoint. If you can't give a real one,
say so and name when you'll have one.

---

## Failure 5 — The work vanished the moment you stopped writing

You said "I'll follow up" or "we should review" or "let's circle
back" in prose, and then nothing existed afterward to hold the
follow-up. By the next run, the thread is gone.

The practice: when an action implies work past the current
moment, materialize it as a separate record per distinct piece of
work and per distinct owner. Title it as a verb plus a subject and
a name. Use the right type — work to be done belongs in a task,
coordinated time belongs on a calendar. Fill in the people
involved; don't leave assignees or invitees blank. Add a one-line
context grounded in what you actually saw.

---

## Failure 6 — You reported success you didn't get

Either the write actually failed and you didn't notice, or the
endpoint replied with something ambiguous and you assumed the best.
Either way, the report says "done" and the state says otherwise.

The practice: if the write response is unambiguous — a returned
ID, an echoed body, a clear status — trust it. If it's thin or
ambiguous, re-read the relevant state to confirm before you claim
success. If a write fails outright, read the error, try one
targeted correction, and if that fails too, stop and report what
went wrong honestly. Don't loop and don't dress failure as
completion.

---

## Failure 7 — You paid the discovery tax twice

You worked out which endpoint did what, which fields were
required, where the useful data sat in the response — and then
the next run starts from zero, paying the same time again.

The practice: when a call works, leave a one-line recipe behind in
`/workspace/learned/`. The shape:

```
TO <goal> → <method> <path>   fields: <required>   response: <where the useful data sits>
```

Plus any non-obvious required fields, error patterns, or response
quirks. Structural facts only — never the names, IDs, or contents
from this run, because next run those will be different and your
note will be wrong. Don't restate the rules in this document.
Don't journal what you did. Merge in place when a recipe already
exists; rewrite when it's been falsified by what you just saw;
prune what's been superseded. The notebook is read at the start of
every run, so every line in it costs attention from then on.

---

## Failure 8 — You ground to a halt waiting for clarity

The task wasn't perfectly specified, you weren't sure which of two
readings to act on, and instead of picking one you stalled. Time
ran out with nothing produced.

The practice: when the intent isn't obvious, name the
interpretation you're going with in a single line and proceed on
it. The line lets a reader correct the choice; the proceeding
means there's something to correct.

---

## What good looks like

A good run reads like someone who showed up, looked at the
situation, did what was needed, and left a small note for the next
person. The output is short, every fact in it is something you can
point at in the data, the right people heard about it and the
wrong people didn't, the work that didn't finish has a record with
a name on it, and the recipe for the next run got a line longer.

Parallelize what doesn't depend on prior results. Spend attention
on what the task actually touches; ignore the rest until it
matters. When in doubt about a fact, an audience, or a scope,
default to saying less.
